newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares rebound after four percent plunge.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares rebound after four percent plunge.

text.p: Bombay shares rebounded in late trade on Monday as investors rushed to cover short positions following a near four percent plunge in prices earlier in the day, analysts said.
An onslaught of disappointing first-half company results and fears of a prolonged slowdown in the economy inspired heavy selling by foreign funds in early trade, the analysts said.
Bombay's benchmark share market index plunged 109.45 points, or 3.7 percent, to an intraday low of 2,856.21, but rebounded to close 35.44 points up at a provisional 3,001.10.
"Speculators got nervous after the index tumbled below 2,900 points and buying support from some local funds made them rush for cover," said a trader at a foreign brokerage.
Analysts said rumours that index-linked stock ITC Ltd was likely to report a better-than-expected first half result of about 1.8 billion rupees ($50.4 million) had also driven prices higher.
After the market close, ITC confirmed market expectations and said net profit rose to 1.81 billion rupees in the six months to September 30, 1996, from 1.41 billion in the same period last year.
A series of disappointing half-year results announced last week, however, have depressed market sentiment. The index had fallen five percent in the week to Friday.
"Increased interest costs and higher inventory costs have hit first half profits of most firms," said Ashok Reddy, in equity sales at ICICI Securities, an affiliate of J.P. Morgan.
Share prices of Grasim, IDBI, Hindalco, Century Textiles, Titan, Century Enka, Essar Steel, Tata Chemicals, Hindustan Motors and Larsen & Toubro took a pounding after results fell below expectations.
Results from India's largest cement maker Associated Cement Co Ltd and textiles firm Bombay Dyeing & Manufacturing Co Ltd due this week were also expected to be disappointing.
Adding to the misery of the local market, auto stocks -- previously the darlings of foreign funds -- have been hit hard by fears of a prolonged economic slowdown.

"Even fancied sectors are not growing at the pace they were. The initial bull run which was led by auto stocks has come full circle," said Partha Roy Choudhary, head of trading at securities firm Peregrine Capital.
India's April-September industrial growth has slowed to an annual 4.8 percent from 12.8 percent in the corresponding period last year, according to official data released last week.
Auto analysts say a slowdown in demand has led to rising inventories which will in turn translate into lower sales in the second half of 1996/97 (April-March).

"Auto stocks are large contributors to the fall. The story of inventories piling up is gaining a fair bit of momentum especially with Bajaj Auto and TELCO," said the head of trading at a European brokerage.
